When Everyday Requests Turn Into Daily Power Struggles

Perhaps simple everyday routines, getting ready for school, turning off a screen, or starting homework, regularly escalate into heated arguments.

Maybe you feel as though you are walking on eggshells in your own home. Small boundaries can trigger intense frustration, refusal, or pushback, leaving both you and your child exhausted.

You may have been told that your child is "just strong-willed", "disrespectful", or "trying to push your buttons". Beneath the conflict, however, many young people are struggling with emotional regulation, frustration tolerance, and communication.

Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) involves a persistent pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative behaviour, and difficulty responding to rules or authority figures.

If these experiences sound familiar, you do not have to manage them alone.

With the right support, families can better understand what is driving the behaviour and explore calmer, more workable ways of responding together.

Could This Be What Your Child Is Experiencing?

All children and teenagers test limits, argue, or push back from time to time as part of normal development. With ODD, these patterns occur much more frequently, persist over months, and create ongoing disruption at home, at school, or with peers.

You may notice that your child:

  • loses their temper quickly or appears easily annoyed and irritable
  • frequently argues with parents, teachers, or other adults
  • actively refuses to follow everyday rules or reasonable requests
  • seems to deliberately annoy or provoke family members or peers
  • struggles to accept responsibility and quickly blames others when things go wrong
  • holds onto resentment or becomes spiteful when upset
  • reacts with intense frustration to small setbacks or changes in routine
  • experiences ongoing conflict with siblings or difficulty maintaining friendships
  • struggles to calm down once an argument or emotional outburst begins

These behaviours do not automatically mean your child has ODD. Similar challenges can be linked to ADHD, anxiety, learning difficulties, sensory overwhelm, trauma, or major life stressors.

A thorough, clinically informed assessment and support pathway can help clarify what is contributing to your child's behaviour and what type of care may be appropriate.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every family reaches out at a different stage.

You may be seeking support because:

  • daily routines and boundaries consistently end in arguments or meltdowns
  • school has raised concerns about your child's behaviour, anger, or peer conflict
  • traditional discipline strategies seem to escalate conflict rather than resolve it
  • your child or teenager struggles to manage anger and frustration
  • you are worried about how ongoing conflict is affecting siblings and family relationships
  • you are wondering whether ODD, ADHD, or another underlying factor may be involved
  • your child has already received a diagnosis and you want practical, evidence-based guidance
  • you feel exhausted, overwhelmed, or unsure how to respond in difficult moments

You do not need to have all the answers before reaching out.

Understanding Oppositional Defiant Disorder

Looking Beneath Defiant Behaviour

Oppositional Defiant Disorder is a recognised behavioural and emotional condition characterised by ongoing patterns of irritability, defiance, and conflict, most often directed toward familiar adults such as parents and teachers.

While the outward behaviour can look like deliberate rebellion, young people experiencing ODD often have a low tolerance for frustration and difficulty regulating strong emotions in the moment.

When a demand feels overwhelming or unfair, their nervous system can shift quickly into a defensive, argumentative response. Once locked into a power struggle, neither the child nor the adult feels heard.

Understanding what sits underneath the behaviour can help families step out of blame and focus on practical, consistent strategies that support calmer interactions.

When Anger and Defiance Affect Everyday Life

ODD can influence several areas of a young person's daily experience.

Angry and Irritable Mood

A child or teenager may seem chronically touchy, easily frustrated, or quick to anger, with emotional reactions that feel disproportionate to the trigger.

Argumentative and Defiant Behaviour

Frequent questioning of rules, negotiating every instruction, and refusing everyday requests can turn routine transitions into prolonged stand-offs.

Frustration Tolerance and Emotional Regulation

Many young people with ODD struggle to recognise when their frustration is building and may need support to develop skills to pause or calm down before reacting.

Accountability and Blame

When something goes wrong, a child may instinctively blame siblings, peers, or adults rather than taking responsibility, often as a way to avoid shame or feeling inadequate.

Social and School Functioning

Difficulty compromising, sharing, or accepting feedback from teachers and peers can place strain on classroom learning and friendships.

Every young person presents differently, and the intensity of these difficulties can vary across home, school, and social settings.

When ODD Affects the Whole Family

The Ripple Effect Across the Household

Persistent conflict does not only affect the child: it places significant strain on the entire family system.

Parents and caregivers often find themselves caught in exhausting cycles of repeating instructions, negotiating boundaries, managing explosive reactions, and fielding phone calls from school.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • chronic parental stress, burnout, or self-doubt
  • frequent tension or disagreements between co-parents about how to respond
  • sibling distress, resentment, or feeling overlooked
  • disrupted family routines around mornings, meals, homework, and bedtime
  • withdrawal from social outings or family activities due to concerns about meltdowns
  • strained parent-child connection where most interactions feel corrective

Experiencing these pressures does not mean you have failed as a parent. Understanding how these cycles operate can help families explore steadier, more sustainable household dynamics.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Supporting Your Child and Your Family

Supporting a child or teenager with oppositional behaviour often works best when both the young person and the adults around them are supported with practical tools.

Depending on your child's age and needs, therapy and parent-focused support may focus on:

  • understanding the triggers and patterns driving oppositional behaviour
  • building practical emotional regulation and anger-management skills
  • developing problem-solving and communication strategies for young people
  • establishing clear, calm, and predictable household boundaries
  • shifting from power struggles toward constructive, consistent responses
  • strengthening positive connection and trust between parent and child
  • supporting co-parenting alignment and reducing family stress
  • collaborating with schools to promote consistent support across settings

The aim is not to change who your child is, but to help them develop healthier ways to express frustration, navigate expectations, and build positive relationships.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With tailored, consistent support, families may begin to notice gradual shifts in everyday interactions.

Depending on your child's individual needs and circumstances, therapy may help a young person:

  • recognise early signs of anger and practise calming strategies
  • communicate needs and disagreements more constructively
  • tolerate frustration and disappointment with less escalation
  • build stronger problem-solving and perspective-taking skills
  • develop healthier friendships and classroom relationships
  • build confidence and self-understanding outside of negative behaviour cycles

At the same time, parents and caregivers may gain clearer strategies for de-escalating conflict, reinforcing positive choices, and supporting calmer communication at home.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Practical Strategies for Home and School

Young people experiencing oppositional behaviour often respond well to calm predictability, clear expectations, and positive reinforcement rather than reactive arguments.

Families may find it helpful to:

  • pick your battles by focusing on core safety and respect boundaries rather than every minor irritation
  • avoid getting drawn into arguments by stating expectations calmly and stepping back from prolonged debates
  • offer structured choices where appropriate so the young person retains a healthy sense of autonomy
  • give advance notice before transitions using clear countdowns or visual schedules
  • notice and reinforce positive behaviour specifically acknowledging cooperation, effort, and calm responses
  • model calm emotional regulation by taking a brief pause yourself before responding to provocations
  • keep rules simple, clear, and consistent across caregivers and, where possible, between home and school
  • protect positive one-on-one connection time unrelated to chores, rules, or correction

Strategies should be tailored to your child's temperament, developmental stage, and family environment.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Children, Adolescents, and Families

Because oppositional behaviour can stem from, or overlap with, different developmental and emotional factors, support is tailored to your child's specific profile.

Psychological Therapy for the Young Person

Evidence-based approaches such as Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and skills-based interventions may help children and teenagers build emotional awareness, anger-management tools, and flexible problem-solving skills.

Parent Guidance and Management Strategies

Parent-focused sessions, grounded in evidence-based behavioural and relational frameworks, can support caregivers in using clear communication, positive reinforcement, and consistent, non-punitive boundaries.

Family Therapy

Family-focused work may help improve communication patterns, align parenting approaches, reduce household tension, and support siblings affected by ongoing conflict.

School Collaboration

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with teachers or school support staff to promote consistent expectations and supportive classroom strategies.

Medical and Paediatric Support

Where co-occurring conditions such as ADHD, significant mood difficulties, or complex behavioural concerns are present, your GP, paediatrician, or child psychiatrist can conduct a medical assessment and discuss whether medical review or broader multidisciplinary healthcare support may be appropriate alongside psychological care.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Finding the Right Pathway for Your Family

When daily life already feels overwhelming, figuring out whether your child needs an assessment, individual therapy, parenting support, or family counselling can feel like another heavy task.

You do not need to have everything worked out before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens carefully to what has been happening at home and school, gathers relevant background information, and helps match your family with an appropriate practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • noticing persistent anger, arguing, or defiance for the first time
  • wondering whether ODD, ADHD, or emotional regulation difficulties may be involved
  • looking for practical parenting strategies to reduce daily conflict
  • seeking support for a teenager struggling with anger and boundaries
  • wanting coordinated care alongside your GP or school

we are here to help you navigate the next step with clarity and respect.

Why Families Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With Families at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for families seeking psychological and allied health support.

Clinically Informed Intake

Thoughtful intake processes help us understand your concerns and identify a suitable clinical pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect families with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose experience aligns with child, adolescent, and family needs.

Family-Focused Coordination

Our administration team assists parents and caregivers with appointment scheduling, intake requirements, and clear communication.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can collaborate with GPs, paediatricians, schools, and other professionals involved in your child's care.

Practical Referral Support

We assist with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate.
